content: An antigen, derived from the term antibody-generating, is a molecule capable of eliciting an immune response under certain conditions. The term originated from the idea that these molecules stimulate the production of antibodies. However, it is now understood that the immune system is not solely composed of antibodies. The modern definition of an antigen includes any substance that can be recognized by the adaptive immune system. Antigens are typically proteins or polysaccharides, and they may include components of microorganisms such as bacterial coats, capsules, cell walls, flagella, fimbriae, and toxins. Lipids and nucleic acids can also act as antigens, but only when they are associated with proteins or polysaccharides. Non-microbial exogenous antigens, such as pollen, egg white, or proteins from transplanted tissues, organs, or transfused blood cells, can also trigger immune responses. A tolerogen is a specific type of antigen that induces immune non-responsiveness due to its molecular structure. If the molecular structure of a tolerogen is altered, it can become an immunogen, capable of stimulating an immune response. An allergen, on the other hand, is a substance that provokes an allergic reaction. This reaction can occur following exposure through ingestion, inhalation, injection, or skin contact. Cells present their antigens to the immune system via histocompatibility molecules. Depending on the type of antigen and the histocompatibility molecule involved, various immune cells can be activated. Origin of Antigens Antigens can be classified based on their origin: Exogenous Antigens Exogenous antigens are those that enter the body from the external environment, such as through inhalation, ingestion, or injection. These antigens are internalized by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) via endocytosis or phagocytosis and are subsequently processed into smaller fragments. The APCs then present these fragments to CD4+ T helper cells using class II histocompatibility molecules on their surface. Certain T cells are specific to the peptide-MHC complex, and upon recognition, they become activated and secrete cytokines. These cytokines, in turn, activate cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), antibody-secreting B cells, macrophages, and other immune components. Endogenous Antigens Endogenous antigens are generated within a cell as a result of normal cellular metabolism or due to infections caused by viruses or intracellular bacteria. These antigens are presented on the cell surface in association with MHC class I molecules. If activated cytotoxic CD8+ T cells recognize these antigens, they release toxins that induce lysis or apoptosis of the infected cell. To prevent cytotoxic T cells from attacking normal cells presenting self-proteins, self-reactive T cells are eliminated during the process of negative selection, which occurs as part of immune tolerance. Autoantigens Autoantigens are typically normal proteins or protein complexes (and occasionally DNA or RNA) that are mistakenly targeted by the immune system in individuals with autoimmune diseases. Under normal circumstances, these antigens should not provoke an immune response. However, due to genetic and environmental factors, immunological tolerance to these antigens is lost in affected individuals. Tumor Antigens Tumor antigens, also known as neoantigens, are antigens presented by MHC class I or II molecules on the surface of tumor cells. Some tumor antigens are exclusively expressed by tumor cells and not by normal cells; these are referred to as tumor-specific antigens (TSAs) and often arise from tumor-specific mutations. More commonly, tumor-associated antigens (TAAs) are expressed by both tumor and normal cells. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes that recognize these antigens may destroy tumor cells before they proliferate or metastasize. Tumor antigens can also appear on the tumor surface in forms such as mutated receptors, which can be recognized by B cells. Nativities of Antigens A native antigen is an antigen that has not yet been processed by an APC into smaller fragments. T cells cannot directly bind to native antigens; they require the antigens to be processed by APCs. In contrast, B cells can be activated by native antigens without prior processing.
